en: The *Babai pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Babai),
according to Sengyou’s catalogue, is an early alternative translation of the *Banzhou sanmei jing* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra) attributed to Master Dao’an.
Thus have I heard:

The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, beneath the Many-Birds Tree, together with a community of five hundred bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had no remaining fetters, whose task was accomplished, whose goal was fulfilled, who had laid down the heavy burden, who had attained their own welfare, who had severed the continuity of rebirth, who had reached the ultimate state, and who had all transcended the eight dhyānas—except for one ordinary bhikṣu.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pāpīyas, together with five hundred bodhisattvas, all of whom were laypeople observing the five precepts, came before the Tathāgata desiring to receive the True Dharma.
Baipei Bodhisattva then rose, went forward to where the Buddha was, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.
All the bodhisattvas and bhikṣus likewise prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and all sat down to one side.

At that time, the Buddha immediately entered the meditative concentration of divine power (*ṛddhi-samādhi*), causing all the bhikṣus who were in other kingdoms and regions to come to this assembly at the Bamboo Grove and pay homage to the Buddha.
At that time, more than one hundred thousand bhikṣus gathered at the Bamboo Grove.

The Buddha again entered a state of meditative concentration involving supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), causing the venerable bhikṣuṇīs and others—more than thirty thousand bhikṣuṇīs in total—to come and assemble at the Bamboo Grove. They paid homage to the Buddha and all sat down to one side.

The Buddha again took up a state of meditative concentration characterized by supernormal power (*ṛddhi-samādhi*), causing the Bodhisattva Raṭṭhapāla to come from the great kingdom of Vesālī; the Bodhisattva Khaṇḍadravya from the great kingdom of Campā; the Bodhisattva Nandaka from the great kingdom of Vārāṇasī; the Bodhisattva Susīma from the great kingdom of Kapilavastu; the Bodhisattvas of the Great Assembly of Leaders and the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from the great kingdom of Śrāvastī; the Bodhisattva Udayin from the great kingdom of Kauśāmbī; and the Bodhisattva Māluṅkyaputra from the great kingdom of Sāṃkāśya. Each arrived with twenty-eight thousand followers, and they all assembled at the Bamboo Grove, where they prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Buddha and sat down to one side.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, together with more than one hundred thousand people, came to where the Buddha was. They all prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.

At that time, the four Great Heavenly Kings, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the Brahmā King, together with immeasurable hosts of devas, all came to where the Buddha was; they paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side.
An incalculable multitude of Śubhakṛtsna devas all came to where the Buddha was, paid their respects, and stood to one side.
Also, the four Asura kings, accompanied by an incalculable host of asuras, all came to where the Buddha was; having paid their respects, they all stood to one side.

Then the Nāga King Dhanada, the Nāga King Śaṅkhapāla, the Nāga King Manasvin, the Nāga King Anavatapta, and the Nāga King Elāpattra, together with an immeasurable multitude of nāgas, came to where the Buddha was. Having paid their respects, they all stood to one side.

At that time, within these three thousandfold worlds, there was no place empty or devoid of beings; they were entirely filled with great and wondrous devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans, from the lower realms up to the Brahma Heaven.
Baipei Bodhisattva then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke:
"I now wish to ask a question; I pray that the Buddha will expound upon it and resolve my difficulties."
The Buddha then said: “Bāpī!
Ask whatever you wish.
I, the Tathāgata, am now able to fully resolve all that you ask, for I know the nature of the arising and ceasing of your thoughts.”

Baipei Bodhisattva then said: "How does one attain the bodhisattva’s concentrated mind, such that what is heard is as vast as the ocean and stored away in abundance; such that in what is heard there is no further doubt; such that one does not forget the arising of mindfulness nor regress; and such that one does not grow indolent regarding the unsurpassed path, the supreme virtue of perfect enlightenment?

How does one take birth as a Buddha, not falling into the realm of non-existence; always knowing the source from which one has come to be born; never departing from one's original vow to behold the Tathāgata; and even when lying down or dreaming, never departing from the correct state?"

One’s physical form will always be upright, handsome, and lovely, bringing joy to all who see it; one will be born into a noble and wealthy family, always maintaining a firm and steadfast mind. One’s internal learning will be swift and what is known will not be forgotten; one’s deliberations will be vast, one’s resolve firm, and one will possess a sense of shame (*hrī-apatrāpya*). One will fully comprehend the marvelous principles and be capable of practicing great compassion. One will always possess silent awakening and, in all encounters, manifest great majestic power (*mahānubhāva*). One will always be diligent without ever regretting one’s efforts;

one will propagate and disseminate the meaning, constantly entering into the Dharma, constantly entering into tranquility (*śamatha*), constantly entering into insight (*vipaśyanā*), constantly entering into *dhyāna*, and constantly entering into meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One will enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without grasping at signs, abiding in the ground of formlessness, and remaining neither terrified nor afraid.

One will always delight in preaching the Dharma and always delight in receiving the Dharma; whatever one wishes for in terms of rebirth will never deviate from one’s original vow. One’s fundamental virtue will be powerful, and one’s fundamental intention will be powerful.

The original causes and conditions are powerful; the five faculties are powerful; what is performed is always powerful; the rebuking and stopping of evil is always powerful; what is contemplated is always powerful; and in the understanding of one's vows, it is always powerful.

His measure is difficult to surpass, like the ocean; he is like the moon, naturally endowed with purity and fullness; he is like the sun, gradually dispelling the darkness; he is like fire, capable of manifesting forms; he is like space, difficult to defile and free from attachment, his mind already empty; he is like a bright jewel, fully realizing the True Dharma; he is like a rock, dwelling securely and immovable; he is like a root, difficult to shake; he is like a soft and supple hide, his mind free from any wound or blemish; he is like a soaring bird, his mind humble and subdued; he is like a beggar who does not rise, finding joy in remote lands and mountain valleys; he is like a deer, a wild ox, or a monkey, having no affection for worldly people.
There are also those in training who constantly lead the multitude and draw others along; they harbor no anger toward anyone.
They do not merely transform others, but liberate all demons in succession. Regarding all dharmas, there is no external instruction, for they understand them through their own minds.

Abiding in awakening within dhyāna, they remain firm and do not rely on the heterodox. Possessing the power of great compassion, they are difficult to disturb, and their contemplation is always profound.
Not departing from right practice, one is unable to calculate what is attained or what is contemplated; upon hearing the enumeration of the Dharma, one sheds tears of faith.
What is avoided is always excessive; one fully possesses the thoughts and vows of the Buddha’s conduct.
When the multitudes come desiring to gather countless wholesome thoughts, they vow to take up the pure faith of the ocean, increasing their vows for purity, free from envy, jealousy, and anger.
Having severed anger, one constantly aspires for the presence of light; with all-knowledge attained, one rejoices within the radiance.
Through the practice of vows, one severs lack of faith and aversion, being sprinkled by wisdom. One fulfills countless heavenly vows and practices;
having severed all worldly finery and vanity, one becomes pure and excellent in conduct, fully endowed with the purity of precepts, and is thus able to sever the causes for discipleship.
Regarding the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, their aspiration for the mind is firm and unshakable; what they do is ultimately accomplished, and that which they seek is eternally without fabrication.
They never tire of practicing wholesome dharmas within the realms of gods and humans; they fully perfect and complete all the *pāramitās* as Bodhisattvas, remaining free from both sorrow and joy.
Toward all heterodox teachings, they are never swayed or biased; they revere and delight in all Buddhas.
One perceives that the radiance of all phenomena cannot be transformed or destroyed, and always encounters all Buddhas face-to-face.
For example, like a person created by illusion, all phenomena are not-self; like a conjured being, one does not come into existence in future dharmas.
It is like the past, future, and present events of a person in a dream; it is like a light by which all worlds see one's own body;
it is like two suns that neither move nor come to rest. Such is the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): it is like a shadow within birth and death.
By abiding in the absence of the womb, one has already severed the perception of the womb; thus, one does not grasp at phenomena (*dharma*).
Practicing the far-reaching path, they have already cast aside anxiety regarding the vessels of the Dharma; the intentions of these Bodhisattvas are already immeasurable.
Nothing in the world can turn them back or cause them to fall; they draw near to non-attachment.

Having already crossed the gate of the tally and seal of all Buddha-fields, they are fully capable of disseminating the wholesome Dharma. From themselves upward, they are like vessels of the Dharma; thus it is with all.
Regarding all Buddhas, he is honored by all Tathāgatas; through the divine power of the Buddha, his hair and pores remain unmoved, and his capability is like the solitary roar of a lion.
He is always seen with reverence by all, able to satisfy the multitudes of the world without confusion or error.
He is known and awaited by all Buddhas, awakening and transforming beings according to the proper time, and casting [them] away [from suffering].
Regarding what is doubted: there is no such thing as receiving dharmas; all that exists across the three periods of time is illuminated and known without exception.
All wise ones speak without end; they constantly practice compassion to attain pity. They do not linger in worldly affairs, but clarify the sutras by abandoning the dwelling of the unwise.
Toward all people, they do not follow two paths; their body and mind arise together in straightforwardness, and their minds act for the sake of the world.
The eye is the illumination of the three realms; throughout the three realms, there is none who can easily surpass it.
Its practice is non-self; all that exists in the world is merely a succession of cessations. In its practice, it seeks no worldly pleasures; it walks alone with faith, mindfulness, and sincerity.

Regarding phenomena, it neither grasps nor rejects, but expounds the teaching of universal knowledge. It exhorts others to abide in the gateway of the Great Vehicle, having already reached the state of non-attainment.
Terror! The Tathāgata’s True Dharma is well-expounded; its every phrase and verse is constantly practiced.
Those who seek to see it find no lack of joy; all those who follow it obtain the joy of great bliss.

Standing at the lotus-feet of the Tathāgata, one should delight in the well-expounded teaching of all Buddha-dharmas, delighting in the practice of inquiry without harboring resentment or attachment toward such conduct.
Within the assembly, he severs all received terrors; he exerts power through speech and action so that all may cross over and transform;
he always directly takes up his dwelling without wavering; amidst all weakness, he assists with the preaching of the Dharma and sits upon the lion throne;
repeatedly, there is that which is known by all Buddhas; remaining in the world, he does not fall into anything, and he fully explains the practice of entering [the path].
Knowing the eternal honor of the Dharma, they follow the practices of all Buddhas; always aspiring to the Dharma without weariness, they wait upon the ignorant.
The Tathāgata’s skillful engagement has no fixed locus; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he constantly delights in practicing all things.
For the sake of others, he causes them to abandon transgressions and achieve merit; silently, his virtues increase daily as he enters the gates of the Dharma, just like the laws of heaven.

Because the body has no form, one constantly restrains the internal person; as a bodhisattva, one never severs any of the Buddha’s practices, does not dwell in desire, and is fully equipped with the armor already donned by the bodhisattvas.

Although there may be many who harbor resentment and jealousy, one desires to surpass them all, repeatedly aspiring toward the Tathāgata’s ten powers and stages, and eliminating all conceptualizations.
Having already attained full knowledge and mastery, he understands through skillful calculation the gathering and dispersing of the world.

All conditioned phenomena enter into birth and death; yet he abandons them, abiding nowhere and remaining undisturbed. Having crossed the ocean of dharmas, he is a treasury of noble jewels; though he moves throughout the world, he has distanced himself from all worldly things.

Having already practiced the great transformations and being fully endowed with the power of a Buddha, which is beyond compare, they concentrate their single-minded resolve to behold all Buddhas; they cast aside and do not employ any worldly realms, yet wherever they are born in various worlds, there Tathāgatas abide, the Perfectly Awakened Ones who are free from attachment.

From afar they see the Buddha and his realm, hear his Dharma, and behold his community of bhikṣus; yet they do not reach there by way of the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), nor do they reach there by way of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā). Furthermore, these bodhisattvas do not depart from this world to go to that world in order to listen or see; they remain in this very world as before.

May they behold the Perfectly Awakened One from afar and hear the luminous Dharma, fully receiving and practicing it just as if they were receiving and practicing it face-to-face now; may they be made equal to me so that I have no doubt, and likewise may all bodhisattvas be free from indolence, constantly seeing the Buddha face-to-face and hearing the Dharma well, such that even in their dreams their minds remain inclined toward nothing but the sublime.
The Buddha then addressed Bodhisattva Bakkula,
saying: "Excellent, excellent, Bakkula!"

This is to express compassion for the multitude, to seek the peace of the multitude, and to take pity upon the three periods of time; seeing what is righteous, seeing what is joyful, and seeing what is peaceful, one is thus able to ask the Tathāgata about such matters for the sake of humans and devas.

In the past, he himself possessed virtue; he had already bestowed manifold blessings upon the Buddhas of the past, had already served and honored the multitude of Buddhas, and sat upon the seat of Dharma and meaning. He made vows for the Dharma without seeking anything for himself, received and upheld the holy life (*brahmacarya*), was of few desires and content with simple sustenance, delighted in being fully endowed with the precepts, and gave rise to all Bodhisattvas. He constantly exhorted others to become Bodhisattvas, always aspired to honor Bodhisattvas, and always wished for the greatness of the Bodhisattva’s mind, for the flourishing of the Bodhisattva, and for the attainment of the Bodhisattva. His aspirations were always characterized by great compassion, relying on a mind of universal equanimity. Toward all people, he practiced the perfection of mental discipline (*cittavīrya-pāramitā*); seeing the Buddhas, he constantly sought the principle of deliverance according to the Tathāgata’s words, aspiring to the intent of Buddhahood.
“Pūrṇa, it is as if there were no measure for the iron of the earth; you have always skillfully known and perceived the conduct of others’ minds—this is your virtue. Pūrṇa!

I already know this fully with my mind. Nevertheless, there is the concentration of a present Buddha called ‘Ever-Abiding. This concentration is the concentrated mind, firm and non-falling, never losing its mindfulness.”

“May the assembly of those with inferior faculties not be negligent; may the Tathāgata alone explain this meditative concentration for us, acting as a leader for those who train, so that all people may attain peace.”
"I pray that you will have compassion for this world, so that humans, devas, and all bodhisattvas who possess great vows may all, by means of this light, see themselves illuminated.
The Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Bopati, saying:
"Constantly practice a single dharma; always act with tireless diligence. Practice as described above; increase your benefits and do not let them diminish."

Just as when a carriage is finished one mounts it and may then pursue whatever one seeks, so too, having perfected purity, having practiced mindful reflection, and having perfected steadfastness, one exerts the fundamental effort to perform all wholesome dharmas; thus one personally attains transcendence and thereby exists.
What is the one dharma that constitutes seeing the Buddha in meditative concentration, which is called "abiding in the stability of cessation"?

It is this: through causes and conditions, the Buddha’s mind forms a thought; his mind is neither perverse nor obscured, nor is it distracted. Having attained silent mastery and diligence, he does not falter; though formless, there is a response to him. He constantly dwells in the profound emptiness even while sleeping; he treats even the most grievous enemies as if they were distant from any assembly. His body always remains hidden, avoiding evil associates and never befriending them; he follows virtuous companions who conform to the Way of the Dharma. With upright faculties, he does not engage in false divination or seek worldly satisfaction; he desires little food and harbors no greed. He is fond of Dharma-robes and does not wish for a long life; following his original destiny and wisdom, his body has nothing to love, and he disregards his kinsmen. He swiftly abandons the land where he was born.

Having cultivated loving-kindness, having attained a compassionate mind, having dwelled in a joyful mind, and having practiced equanimity; having abandoned all hindrances, practiced all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and discerned the perception of form; not grasping at the perception of the aggregates (*skandha*), not clinging to the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and not harboring views regarding the great elements (*mahābhūta*); with a mind that no longer gives rise to distraction, not dwelling upon impurity in sensation, and having attained universal equanimity; turning toward the liberation of all beings, regarding all people as one’s own self, and realizing that all people are not "self"; with no grasping toward any phenomena (*dharma*), making no wishes beyond the precepts, constantly practicing the concentration of desire, delighting in extensive learning, with the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*) free from leakage or violation, the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*) unshakable and non-falling, having no further doubt regarding the Dharma, being without contention with the Buddha, not rejecting the Dharma, and not slandering the Sangha.

Harsh and abusive speech is cut off and brought to rest; one treats others with the Way. One always keeps far away from transgressions; worldly sounds are neither sought nor enjoyed, while sounds beyond the world are always cherished and delighted in; the cries of animals are cast far away and avoided.

Having practiced the six steadfast dharmas, one should constantly practice the five deliverances; having fully abandoned the ten unwholesome actions, one should fully cultivate the ten wholesome actions. Being able to liberate oneself from the nine afflictions, one should entirely reject the eight powerless states. Having constantly practiced the eight kinds of diligence and performed the nine contemplations, one should have attained the eight recollections of the noble ones. Regarding the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), do not grasp at them with craving, and do not become arrogant on account of what you have heard.

The principle may be subtle; listen with focused ears. Always revere the Dharma, always desire the Dharma. Having distinguished the perception of form, one’s own body is no longer grasped; having completely relinquished the perception of persons, though one is born, one does not act for the sake of [existence]. Having analyzed the perceptions of the aggregates (*skandha*), one no longer dwells in anything that exists; constantly seeking Nirvana, one vows not to engage in the cycle of birth and death.

One should conceive of birth and death as fear; perceive the aggregates (*skandha*) as enemies; regard the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as snakes; contemplate the sense bases (*āyatana*) as empty; conceive of the three realms as having no place of abiding; and, beholding *nirvāṇa*, find solitary joy therein.

One ceases worldly activities and no longer employs them; abandoning the world, one follows the Buddha, ensuring there is no contention with others. One has no personal attachments to anything in the world and constantly beholds the faces of all Buddhas. Possessing this body as if seeing it in a dream, one is oriented toward liberation. Always pure and virtuous in action, one constantly seeks out all mental conceptions, discerning and establishing the three certainties. Constantly fixing the mind upon all Buddhas, relying upon and adhering to the roots of goodness, one always contemplates and aspires to all Buddhas.

Mastery over meditative concentration at will; not aspiring for the marks and signs of a Buddha’s body; non-discrimination regarding all phenomena; understanding the meaning of worldly conventions without contention; following the sequential capacity arising from reception; abiding in the ground of benefit according to the Tathāgata; having attained patience and below, entering the emptiness of the Dharma-body; knowing that the human body is neither born nor extinguished, the Nirvāṇa-body; and constantly purifying it through the eye of wisdom and contemplation.

All phenomena are without self; may the Buddha’s intention neither fall short nor exceed [its aim]. May all things be unified in their conduct toward the Buddha, without conceptualizing or seeking to attain anything, thereby extending and straightening the mind for the sake of immeasurable consciousnesses.

Acting for the sake of [enlightened] deeds and not for their opposites; following the Buddha’s wisdom and meeting virtuous friends as if seeing the Honored One; maintaining no divergent thoughts toward any bodhisattvas—all such actions are contrary to the works of Māra.

All that exists in the world is like an illusion; all Buddhas are like light. Perceiving the Tathāgata, one constantly practices with the intent of a bodhisattva, attaining the infinite and universal equality of the billions of sincere faiths through which one beholds all Buddhas and all equal wholesome dharmas.
“Bāpī! This is the concentration of mind that dwells before the face of the present Buddha; it is also by means of this concentration of mind that one brings forth the perfection of this Dharma.
What is the concentration of mind that brings forth the perfection of this Dharma?”
Regarding that which is called "the present":
what is the state of meditative concentration in which the Buddhas of the present dwell face-to-face? Bāpī!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who are always fully endowed with the precepts and constantly dwell alone rather than in the company of others, they may give rise to this thought:
"In which direction does Amitābha Buddha currently reside and constantly preach the Dharma?"
According to what he had heard, he then conceived the thought that it was in the west, the realm governed by the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, Amitābha Buddha.

This Buddha-land lies beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds; it is named the Land of Supreme Bliss (Sukhāvatī), where a multitude of bodhisattvas gather. Having listened to the preaching of the Honored One without distraction, one should always keep this land in mind.

“Bāpī! It is like a person who, while lying down and dreaming, sees heaps of silver, gold, and various treasures, as well as friends, acquaintances, and beloved relatives whom they always delight in seeing and never tire of; they then play and enjoy themselves with them, conversing with them with sincere intimacy.”
Upon waking, one still remembers what was seen and describes it to others as if it were a real event, even shedding tears as one recalls those perceptions.

Bapoi! It is just so for a lay bodhisattva or a practitioner who hears of the land where Amitābha Buddha resides: they should constantly keep that direction in mind, remain without any breach or flaw in their precepts, and never allow their minds to be distracted regarding the aggregate of morality (śīlaskandha). With a pure heart, they should practice mindfulness for one day and night, up to seven days and seven nights. Having completed such mindfulness for seven days and seven nights, they shall be able to see Amitābha Buddha; whether in a dream or while awake, they will behold the Tathāgata Amitābha face-to-face.

For example, it is like a man in a dream who imagines himself dwelling in empty space; he does not think of night nor does he think of day, and his faculty of sight is neither obstructed by walls nor obscured by darkness.

Bāpī! It is the same for a bodhisattva who practices with such mental attention: even if there are Mount Sumerus, Mount Cakravāḍas, Mount Mahācakravāḍas, and other black mountains within the intermediate space of the Buddha-fields, they cannot obstruct his vision, nor can they obstruct his mind.
The Bodhisattva has not yet attained the divine eye to behold Amitābha Buddha;
nor has he attained the divine ear to hear Amitābha Buddha preaching the sutras;
nor has he yet attained the power of spiritual travel to go to the land of Amitābha Buddha.

The bodhisattva likewise does not pass away from this world to be reborn there; rather, while remaining in this world, he beholds the Tathāgata Amitābha Buddha and hears his preaching of the Dharma, which he then practices exactly as heard. From that state of meditative concentration, the bodhisattva awakens and, in accordance with the Dharma he has heard, expounds it extensively for others.

“Bāpī! It is as if there were a man who, having heard from Sūśali that there was a beautiful woman named Suvarṇavarṇā, and another second man who had heard of a beautiful woman named Āvanti, and yet another third man who had heard of a beautiful woman named Utpalavarṇā—having heard these things from one to another, they became attached, their minds grew defiled, and they conceived greed. Although none of these men had ever seen the women, merely by hearing of them repeatedly, their intentions arose and thoughts were born; thus lust arose within them. While lying down, they saw her in dreams, and they went directly to the women’s dwellings.”

Therefore, the men in the city of Rājagṛha conceived such thoughts and saw such things; they came together and engaged in sexual intercourse, and because they awakened at dawn, they recognized it as it was asked and knew it as it was.

Bāpī! For your sake I have spoken thus; from these causes and conditions, such is the teaching of the Dharma. From this state of non-returning, one receives a distinction regarding the path to unsurpassed enlightenment. I further declare for him that in the distant future, he shall be named Saṃbuddha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. That person shall attain the freedom of views and perceptions, such as right view.
In this way, Bakkula! It is also thus for a bodhisattva dwelling in this world:

having heard of that Amitābha Buddha and having contemplated him repeatedly, they then see the Tathāgata Amitābha present before them. Seeing the Buddha’s face, they abide in a state of superior meditative concentration (*adhyātmasamādhi*). Having seen him, they then question the Tathāgata: "By means of which Dharma assembly do bodhisattvas attain birth in this world?"
Amitābha Buddha then spoke to the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Constantly mindfulness of the Buddha with a mind that practices well and does not abandon it, and always acting through the creation of illusion—by this one shall attain birth in this Buddha-land."
"What is meant by 'constantly recollecting the Buddha'?
It is to recollect the Dharma of the Tathāgata without forgetting.

This present one is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One; his body possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, with a body the color of purple-polished gold, like a pure bright moon or a crystal bead."
For example, like one adorned with necklaces of various jewels who alone preaches the Dharma among the assembly of disciples—this is how he speaks with sincerity.

Why? Because there is nothing that can be destroyed. What is it that cannot be destroyed or ruined? Earth, water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and Brahmā Kings—all these do not perish; their form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness remain as they are. To thus recollect the Tathāgata, wherein causes and conditions are like space, and space is already attained—this is the intention of mindfulness of the Buddha. The Bodhisattva, being constantly awake, has already relinquished his meditative concentration.

Bāpī! You should go to that place immediately; upon arriving, speak these matters as they are according to this Dharma teaching, so that he may receive his prediction and no longer fall back, but attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
Bāpī! It is you, as well as Mahākāśyapa, the Bodhisattva Indradatta, the Devaputra Susīma, and others who have attained realization through this concentrated state of mind.

“Bāpī! Long ago in the distant past, there was a man who, while in a vast wilderness, became both extremely hungry and thirsty. He lay down in the marsh and dreamed that he obtained fine food and ate his fill to his heart’s content, so that his hunger and thirst were satisfied.”
Upon waking, one perceives that the body is full; one should then reflect upon this phenomenon as being like eating in a dream. Observing it in this way, one accepts it with detachment.

Regarding the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas within the Buddha-dharma, whether at home or in study, when one hears of the direction in which the Buddha resides, one should always direct the mind toward that quarter and constantly aspire to see the Buddha. Do not form conceptions of a womb, nor do you conceive of having a self-body; dwell constantly in the perception of emptiness. When there is a perception, you should perceive the Buddha. By abiding through the perception of emptiness and by being able to perceive the Buddha—the Honored One among men, pure as lapis lazuli—one will thus see the Tathāgata through such mindfulness.

“Bāpī! It is like a person who has gone from his native land to another country; after a long time, he remembers the games and sights of his birthplace. While lying down in pleasure, he dreams of returning to his old country and plays there, perceiving it as the place he had previously reached, and frolics at will within that kingdom.”
Upon waking, he would speak to his intimates, acquaintances, and attendants, saying: "I went thus; I saw thus; that which I reached and that which I performed was thus."

Pabai! It is the same for a bodhisattva: whether living at home or as a student, upon hearing the direction in which the Buddha resides, they should constantly keep that direction in mind and always aspire to see the Buddha.
Reflecting thus, the Bodhisattva beholds the Tathāgata, pure as a supreme Vaidūrya jewel. "Pāpīyaṇa!

It is like a bhikṣu contemplating impurities who takes a half-decayed corpse and places it before him; having seen it, he sees its blue-black color and its decay; it becomes empty like smoke until he sees only white bones before him. From where did these bones come?"
Who grasps this? Who creates this?
It is all created by the mind alone.

Bāpī! It is the same for the bodhisattva: holding fast to the Buddha and not turning elsewhere, they abide in this state of meditative concentration. Whichever direction they turn toward with skillful means and the aspiration to see the Buddha, if there is a Buddha in that direction, they immediately behold the body of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because they rely upon and are attached to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, because they have already taken hold of the Buddha, they abide in this concentration; through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*), their own power of concentration, and the deeds performed by their own past merit, these three causes enable them all to see the Tathāgata.

“Bāpī! It is, for example, like a person who is still young, who delights in wiping clean vessels to receive sesame oil, receiving clear water in clean vessels, or polishing a mirror anew; if they were to look at their own body in a crystal vessel, they would see their form reflected within all of them.”
“Bāpī! Would you say that this human form enters into oil, water, a mirror, or a crystal vessel?
Or is it already within them?”
He replied, "No, Tathāgata."

I say that it is not found internally; yet when sesame oil, water, a mirror, or crystal are placed before one, the reflection appears as if dwelling right there. It does not come from the light, nor does it emerge from within the body.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Bāpī!"
It is indeed so.

Because they have already distinguished pure form (*rūpa*), when bodhisattvas wish to see the Buddha, it is easy and without difficulty; upon seeing him, they are able to ask questions, and having asked, they receive answers. Hearing what they have heard, they rejoice within, and further reflect thus:
"From where do these Buddhas come?"
"Where have I gone? All these things have no place from which they come; thus one knows that the Tathāgata has no place from which he departs.
It is said that one's own self arises again from the mind; it is merely the activity of the mind that constitutes these three realms."
When I wish to perceive the heavens, my mind immediately sees the heavens; when I manifest as a Buddha by means of the mind, it is likewise perceived through the mind, yet this is merely my own mind.
To become a Buddha-Tathāgata is simply a matter of the mind, as well as the mind of my own body.

When the mind perceives the Buddha, the mind cannot see the mind, and the mind cannot know the mind; the conceptualization of the mind is ignorance, while the non-conceptualization of the mind is nirvāṇa.

"These dharmas have no solidity; they all arise from what is self-conceivable (*sva-vedya*), and that which is self-conceivable is entirely empty. Even when one seeks that which is self-conceivable, it is not to be found.
Pāpīya! The Bodhisattva likewise abides in this samādhi."
“Bāpī! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi. What are the four?
First is boundless faith; second is diligence that cannot be surpassed; third is wisdom that does not accept their teachings; fourth is associating with virtuous friends. Pāpīya!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are another four dharmas by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi:
constantly seeking to see the Buddha; constantly aspiring to hear the Dharma; reckoning that there is nothing upon which to dwell; and never forgetting the intent to seek the Buddha.
By means of these four dharmas, a bodhisattva swiftly attains this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas. What are these four?

He takes no pleasure in worldly talk, takes no pleasure in being recognized by others, does not desire worldly pleasures, and does not indulge in sleep or reclining, except for the times of relieving himself, eating, and walking in meditation.
Not seeking out the fourfold assembly or other crowds, but constantly increasing the giving of the Dharma, and taking no pleasure in fine forms or waiting for excessive gain—
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one quickly attains this samādhi:
constantly fashioning images of the Buddha and next painting their beautiful forms;

constantly maintaining the intent of this samādhi, as well as delighting in this samādhi with the mind so that it abides for a long time in stillness; and likewise writing it down, receiving it, and practicing it accordingly.
This concentration arises when one abandons frivolous and agreeable things, as well as frivolous and agreeable dharmas, and dwells in the unsurpassed, solitary, and sovereign path;
one constantly upholds and protects the Tathāgata’s teaching, remaining true and never forgetting it.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva quickly attains this samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha, knowing this meaning, spoke in verse:
"One should give rise to faith in the Honored One’s teaching; Do not fear what is spoken of as emptiness in the Dharma."
Exerting diligence, cut off reclining; for three full months, one should practice sitting meditation.
Constantly preach the Dharma spoken by the Honored One, and specifically instruct others to manifest its merit.
Do not delight in attachment to views or worldly treatment; being free from all attachments, one attains this Dharma.
With the purple-golden hue of a hundred blessings, always manifesting the Buddha as if standing before one;
with joyful light illuminating all, his form is exquisitely beautiful like a golden pearl.
Regarding the Buddhas of the past and the future, one should always maintain mindfulness with palms joined in reverence.
I also see those who dwell as lords among men, all reverently mindful of the sublime Dharma;
they constantly attend upon the King of Virtue, scattering flowers and incense over his form,
and always offering food and drink with a pure mind— if one seeks this samādhi, how could it be difficult?
With the beating of drums and the playing of lutes and zithers, they constantly perform immeasurable music,
creating countless joys and delights, always aspiring to seek the ultimate samādhi.

Constantly creating peerless forms, Skilled in discerning the marks and endowed with excellence, With a golden body, he pays homage to the Pure One; What difficulty could there be in his vows and concentration?
He constantly contemplates the Dharma as it is contemplated, Seeking pure precepts and the desire for learning.
Accompanied by affairs, the assembly perishes and scatters; thus, the attainment of concentration will not be long delayed.
Do not give rise to affliction regarding that which has form; practice a compassionate mind and rely fully upon protection.
Furthermore, contemplate that desires are both pleasant and painful; seek this concentration, and its attainment will not be long delayed.
One should take joy in preaching the Dharma; attend upon the Honored One with constant reverence.
Abandon frivolity and cast away greed and stinginess; do not treat the teaching of the Dharma with haste or mockery.
Thus, one should make the wholesome wait; that which arises and ceases has been taught by the Tathāgata.
All the countless Buddhas have likewise instructed: do not find difficulty in the concentration you seek.

“Bāpī! A bodhisattva should show reverence toward a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma; they should always honor and attend to him as if he were a venerable one, and in this way, their concentration will progress.”
Bāpī! There are bodhisattvas who, when a bhikṣu preaches the sūtras, have distracted minds; they harbor thoughts of jealousy, resentment, and hatred, and lack a pure heart. Bāpī!

This is not what is contained in the [non-Buddhist] scriptures; they would have to admit that a bodhisattva can attain this state of meditative concentration and reach the fullness of the honored Way, but such a principle simply does not exist.
Pabai! It is like a man with sight who, on a clear night free of clouds and mist, looks up at the sky at midnight and sees countless stars.

Bāpī! It is the same for a bodhisattva who, while receiving and protecting the Buddha-dharma, contemplates the mind. In the eastern direction, they see countless Buddhas—countless hundreds, countless thousands, countless tens of thousands, and countless billions of hundreds of thousands. To seek and behold them is extremely easy; they are seen by the observation of the visual faculty.
Pobai! Just as the Tathāgata’s eye of perfect enlightenment knows all and sees all, so too is the bodhisattva:

they see the Buddha dwelling here in right concentration; they practice the perfection of hearing from illusion, they practice the perfection of unyielding diligence, they practice the perfection of giving, they practice the perfection of the precepts, they practice the perfection of patience, they practice the perfection of meditative intent, they practice the perfection of wisdom-concentration, they attain the perfection of liberating wisdom, and they practice the perfection of unsurpassed wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha, in order to explain this meaning, spoke these verses:
"With eyes looking upward at the sky, Rising in the middle of the night when the moon is pure, One sees countless billions of *yojanas*;
Though it is bright with dawn, the mind remains fixed on consciousness."
When a bodhisattva attains such concentration of mind, they behold countless thousands of Buddha-fields;
through awakening from that concentration, they recognize them and also describe the excellences of those lands to the assembly.
Next, with the eye of meditative concentration purified, he perceives clearly; Unobstructed, he beholds the ten directions.
This supreme and lovely state is the awakened eye; Through the purity of this concentration, he sees the Honored One.
The Honored One contemplates the world without regard for time; He beholds the Honored Ones of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Having severed the poisons, he is pure and free from the marks of rebirth; I pray that you will listen to this virtuous student of supreme merit.
Listening to the Dharma is also most refreshing; one should quickly contemplate emptiness as the essential practice.
May I be joined with this Dharma-vow, and may all beings find peace and become Buddhas.
Just as there are the forms of immeasurable bodhisattvas, And one sees hundreds of millions of Buddha-lands,
So too, after the bodhisattva has attained this samādhi, He beholds the infinite forms of the Honored Ones.

Those who aspire to learn universal loving-kindness and benevolence, And having heard it from me, uphold and practice it in its entirety— It is these bodhisattvas who attain this samādhi; They do not grasp at hundreds of countless dharmas.
Faith, shame, and remorse give rise to perception and craving; abandon all that the world deems desirable.
Why not practice the giving of worldly dharmas? From this, one attains the ground of pure stillness.
“Bāpī! When a bodhisattva has attained meditative concentration, he should arise from that concentration and generate diligence.

It is like a ship filled with various treasures that has already crossed the great ocean and reached this shore, only for the ship to sink near the bank. At that time, the people of Jambudvīpa would raise their voices in great lamentation, crying out in resentment and weeping in sorrow.”
"We are already poor and do not see any fine jewels. Bāpī!

From that point on, when the concentration of mind has been heard and long since passed away, they will no longer write it, read it, recite it, or practice it; nor will they seek its meaning. Monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen throughout that land, as well as all the devas and the world, will all raise their voices in great lamentation and cry out in sorrow:

"We have all become utterly impoverished; the assembly has not seen this Dharma-gift. Although there already exists this profound and subtle meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which was personally taught by the Buddha, praised by the Buddha, and esteemed by the Buddha, we have heard it and yet did not commit it to writing, nor did we memorize it, nor read it, nor practice it, nor abide in it. We delight in listening to flowery rhetoric that harms wisdom; we do not wish to hear it in its entirety, nor do we seek to acquire great knowledge. Though we have heard it, we have no desire for it, nor do we take pleasure in acquiring this concentration."
“Bāpī! It is like a foolish person of little intelligence. Suppose someone comes and gives him sandalwood; the fool conceives an impure thought toward it, whereupon the wise man says to him:
‘This sandalwood is of the finest fragrance; why do you conceive an impure thought toward it?’”
"Why do you not smell it to perceive its fine fragrance?
Why do you not look at it to see its beautiful color?
He then pinched his nose because he did not wish to smell the fragrance, and closed his eyes because he did not wish to see the fragrance and the color.

When this samādhi is being taught, it is likewise so: those who lack precepts do not delight in distancing themselves from desire, nor do they delight in receiving and practicing it; those who lack wisdom lose their intelligence through suffering. Upon reaching dhyāna, they become attached to it and return to the womb. When such people hear of this samādhi-mindfulness, they neither believe in it, nor employ it, nor follow it, nor give rise to inner joy. Furthermore, they utter these words aloud before the assembly, making this vow: "Excellent!"
"If even those who now study the *Prabhāsa* [Sūtra] can achieve such results, then there are currently eminent bhikṣus in this world, such as Ānanda.

This sūtra is like a deceptive melody; having departed from the assembly, it was preached in a secluded place and is not the truth. This sūtra is intended to mislead the ears of those who wish to hear it with craftiness; it was not spoken by the Buddha."
“Bāpī! It is like a merchant who goes to the side of a foolish and ignorant person and takes out an exquisite maṇi jewel to show it to that deluded man.
This foolish man asks the owner:”
"How much is the value of this pearl?
The owner replied,
"If one were to fill the area illuminated by such a pearl at night with precious gems, that would be its value among the ranks of merchants."
He then laughed and mocked the owner of the jewel, and having appraised the *maṇi* gem, he spoke again to the merchant:
"This jewel is worth less than a single ox-load of treasure; that should be its price."

“Bāpī! It is likewise with this samādhi of a bodhisattva in the future. Suppose there is a bhikṣu who can maintain firm faith and has a great desire for learning; who straightforwardly practices and is ashamed of doubt; who seeks liberation through much hearing and possesses wisdom; and who, through deep mindfulness, practices loving-kindness and attains compassion—this samādhi is the state of mastery, and such a samādhi is said to be capable of long endurance.”

Those who are deluded have never previously practiced what is superior to their past faults, nor have they ever possessed merit. They are full of self-conceit and great envy; they seek profit for themselves and desire worldly fame. Having heard little and lacking fundamental training in the good, such people, upon hearing this samādhi, neither uphold it, nor believe in it, nor practice it, nor joyfully accept it.
Furthermore, they utter these words: "This is truly strange!"
How can these bhikṣus not feel shame?
How can these bhikṣus not understand?
Having heard such worldly clever speech, elegant phrasing, and forced arguments, they claim these are the words spoken by the Buddha.
"Vāṣpa! I have now intentionally repeated this for you, so that you and the world of devas and humans may clearly understand it. Vāṣpa!"

If there were someone who, with these three thousandfold world systems filled with the seven treasures, made offerings to all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, yet had not heard of this samādhi;
and if there were a bodhisattva who, having heard of this samādhi, spoke of it after hearing it—this latter merit alone would be far greater.
At that time, the Buddha, having explained this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Even if one were to give away all the three thousandfold worlds, filled entirely with precious jewels,
and practice such deeds as these in the hope of becoming a Buddha, one would still never be peerless and without equal in the world."
Those who are able to obtain this sutra, Whose well-concentrated minds are honored by the Buddhas,
Who hear it and immediately believe, accept, and practice it, And whose merit is swift, solitary, and most supreme.
Flatterers with sycophantic minds are ever self-righteous; their thoughts are gathered in perversity, lacking any root of stability.
They constantly seek out association with evil associates, teaching one another not to believe in this [Dharma].
Leaking of the defilements and devoid of precepts, they are fully possessed of unwholesome dharmas; content in themselves, they remain firmly established in ignorance.
They deceive one another, claiming [the teaching] can be abandoned; they dare to destroy and subvert the supreme instruction.
"This sutra was not spoken by the Buddha," they say; "even the Dharma King never uttered such words.
They dare to produce these evil sounds and speak thus, committing misdeeds without restraining their minds.
There shall be those who behold the Great Hero, Honored One, whose light shall illuminate the three times boundlessly;
for such as these this meaning has appeared, and they all study to uphold the Dharma.
Having heard this profound and wondrous sutra, one receives it upon hearing and gives rise to joy within;
such as these should have no doubts, for they need not worry that they will not become Buddhas in the future.
Those who possess the precepts and pure conduct, who have faith and are entirely upright without deceit,
whose speech flows like the ocean— these are the ones I call "noble."
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Pāpīyaṃs (Babai Pusa Jing)
